title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about writing as a member of your discipline. By now you can work through the writing process and get a draft structured and clear. The step this course takes is different. It treats academic writing not as one universal skill but as a practice shaped by the field you write in.

By the end you will be able to explain how writing conventions vary across disciplines and characterise your own, appraise published writing to work out its conventions, and integrate sources with a critical edge so that your writing advances an argument of your own.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how writing conventions vary across disciplines and characterise those of your own
appraise published writing in your discipline to work out its conventions
integrate sources with a critical edge so that your writing advances your own argument.

title: In real academic practice
body: Writing within your discipline is what the later stages of a degree reward, and what professional and research writing demand. Every essay, report, dissertation chapter and journal submission is judged partly on whether it reads like the work of someone inside the field. The conventions you learn to recognise and adopt here are the ones your markers already use, mostly without naming them.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, that writing is situated in your discipline: why there is no single academic writing, and how fields differ. Second, reading your discipline as a writer: how to work out a field's conventions from the writing already published in it. Third, a critical edge: integrating sources so they serve your own argument, and signalling where you are being critical. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can explain how writing conventions vary across disciplines and characterise those of my own.
I can appraise published writing in my discipline to work out its conventions.
I can integrate sources with a critical edge so that my writing advances my own argument.

title: Orientation
body: 'Academic writing' sounds like one thing you either can or cannot do. It is not. The writing a chemist is marked on and the writing a historian is marked on follow different rules, and a sentence that works in one can fail in the other. This lesson is about that difference: why writing is situated in a discipline, and what that means for how you write.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are past the stage of learning the writing process itself. What is new here is a shift in how you see writing. It is not a general competence you carry between modules unchanged, but a set of conventions that belong to a field and that you take on as you join it. The aim is to recognise those conventions and start reading your own discipline through them.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain why there is no single, monolithic 'academic writing', and why conventions are situated in a discipline
analyse how two disciplines differ in style, vocabulary and structure
identify the conventions that shape writing in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Research into writing at university is clear that writing cannot be taught, or improved, apart from the discipline it belongs to (Halliday and Hasan, 1985; Somerville and Creme, 2005). Each field defines its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure, and even a broad subject such as history divides into sub-fields with their own ways of writing. 'Academic writing' is not one monolithic thing sitting above every subject.

This matters because your writing is judged against the conventions of your field, not against a universal standard. A spare, impersonal register rewarded in one science can read as evasive in a discipline that expects you to argue in your own voice. Recognising that conventions are local, and local to your field, is the first move in writing as a member of it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a recent piece you wrote in your own subject. Which features of it belong to your discipline rather than to writing in general? Name one convention your field expects that another field might not.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Academic writing is not one skill but many, each situated in a discipline that sets its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure. You can now explain why there is no monolithic academic writing, analyse how two fields differ, and begin to identify the conventions of your own. The next lesson turns recognition into method: how to work those conventions out from the writing your discipline already publishes.

title: Orientation
body: If conventions are local to your field, where do you learn them? Rarely from a rulebook. They are carried in the writing your discipline already publishes, and the way to learn them is to read that writing as a writer: not only for what it says, but for how it is made.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You already read widely for content. The move here is to read the same sources a second way, attending to the choices a writer made, so that the conventions stop being invisible and become something you can name and reuse. This is how experienced writers keep learning a field they are still joining.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: explain how to read published work in your discipline as a writer, not only for its content
appraise a piece of writing against the aspects that reveal a discipline's conventions
choose what to notice in a text in {{context}} to work out an unfamiliar convention.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Getting to know how knowledge is articulated in your discipline is something you do deliberately, by reading the writing already published in it. The aim is not to copy, but to notice the choices that recur: how the writer uses vocabulary, how sentences and paragraphs are built, how sources are brought in, and how far the writer appears in the text.

Reading as a writer means asking, of a piece you admire, what makes it work here. Which features belong to this field rather than to writing in general? Over time these observations become a picture of your discipline's conventions that you can write towards, rather than a set of rules someone else has to hand you.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Pick a piece of published writing you rate in your field. Reading it as a writer, what is one choice its author made that you could adopt in your own work?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: Conventions are learned by reading your discipline as a writer: reading well-regarded work a second time for how it is made, noticing what recurs, and writing towards it. You can now explain that way of reading, appraise a piece against the aspects that reveal its conventions, and choose what to notice in an unfamiliar text. The final lesson puts this to work on the hardest convention of all: writing with a critical edge.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 138 to 145 of Chapter 9, 'Writing for assessment', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: Writing within your discipline is not only about matching its style. It is about using sources so that they serve an argument of your own, and making clear where your own judgement is at work. A piece can be fluent and correct and still read as a string of other people's views. A critical edge is what turns it into your argument.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You can already find, quote and reference sources accurately. What this lesson adds is control: deciding what a source is doing in your paragraph, and signalling to the reader where you are weighing it rather than merely reporting it. That control is what markers mean when they ask for a critical edge.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: adapt the 'voices' technique to your discipline's conventions so that a source serves your own argument
appraise how the language of criticality is used in your discipline to signal critical judgement
evaluate, against the conventions of {{context}}, whether a paragraph uses a source to advance an argument or merely reports it

title: Concept: definition
body:
Integrating a source means using it, not just citing it, so that it supports or extends an argument that is yours. One reliable way to do this is the 'voices' technique. The paragraph opens in your own voice with a clear statement of its point; sources are then brought in to support, qualify or complicate that point; and the paragraph closes in your voice with what you make of them.

A critical edge is the second half of this. Being critical begins the moment you pick up a source, but the reader only sees it if you flag it. Using the language of criticality, by weighing, questioning and judging in your own sentences, signals where your argument is doing critical work rather than reporting what others have said.

At this level the moves themselves are familiar; what is new is appraising and adapting them to your own discipline's conventions, since how a field integrates sources and signals criticality is itself a convention.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at a paragraph of your own that used a source. Did the source serve your argument, or did it take over? What is one sentence you could add in your own voice to show your judgement?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
body: A critical edge comes from controlling what a source does in your writing. The 'voices' technique frames each paragraph in your own voice and uses sources to serve its point, while the language of criticality signals where you are weighing rather than reporting. You can now integrate a source this way, flag your criticality, and tell writing that advances an argument from writing that only reports. With conventions recognised, learned and put to work, you can write as a member of your discipline.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Writing within your discipline is no longer a vague aim: it is something you can recognise, learn and do. You can explain why there is no single academic writing, and characterise the conventions of your own field. You can appraise published work as a writer to work those conventions out. And you can integrate sources with a critical edge, using the 'voices' technique and the language of criticality so that your writing advances an argument of your own. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, writing as a member of your discipline is something you practise in every assignment. Each time you match a field's conventions, work them out from what you read, or use a source to serve your own argument, you are doing the work this course named. It is also what research and professional writing reward: the ability to write as an insider, with judgement that is visibly your own.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 136 to 181 of Chapter 9, 'Writing for assessment', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: How three disciplines write
body: Three disciplines, three sets of conventions. Review each card to see how the writing differs.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Chemistry
_items.subtitle: Report the work, not yourself
_items.text: Scientific writing favours a spare, precise vocabulary and often the passive voice. The method and results are foregrounded and the writer stays in the background. Structure follows a fixed order, and each claim is tied tightly to the data.

_items.title: History
_items.subtitle: Argue in your own voice
_items.text: Historical writing is built as an argument. The writer is present, making a case in continuous prose and weighing evidence against interpretation. Vocabulary is rich rather than technical, and structure follows the logic of the argument, not a set template.

_items.title: Education
_items.subtitle: Link practice to theory
_items.text: Writing in primary education moves between classroom practice and the theory that frames it. It is reflective and applied, using observation as evidence, and its structure is shaped by the need to connect what happened to what research says.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two final-year students make the same point, that a result should be read with caution, for an assignment in their discipline.

{{learner-a}} writes it the way it would be written in any subject: 'I think this result is quite interesting, but I am not sure we can fully trust it.' The point is there, but the register is generic and personal. In a field that expects claims to be tied to evidence and the writer kept in the background, it reads as informal and unsupported, whatever its merits.

{{learner-b}} writes the same caution in the conventions of the field: 'The effect is sizeable, but its basis in a single setting limits how far it can be generalised.' The judgement is identical. What differs is that {{learner-b}} has adopted the field's vocabulary, its restraint, and its habit of grounding a claim in a specific limitation. It reads as the work of someone inside the discipline.

Both students reached the same judgement. Only {{learner-b}} expressed it in the conventions the discipline is marked against.

title: Reading for conventions
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these questions to characterise the conventions of writing in a field. Try them on a piece in your own discipline.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: How visible is the writer? Do they argue in their own voice, or stay in the background?
Is the vocabulary technical and spare, or rich and discursive?
Does the structure follow a fixed template, or the logic of an argument?
How closely are claims tied to data, evidence or sources?
What counts as evidence here: results, texts, observation, something else?
Which of these features would read as wrong in a different discipline?

title: Formative check: no single academic writing
displayTitle: Why is it misleading to talk about 'academic writing' as a single skill?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it misleading to treat academic writing as a single skill?

_items.text: Because each discipline sets its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure.
_items.feedback: Yes. Writing is situated in a field, and its conventions are local to that field.

_items.text: Because some students write well and others do not, whatever the subject.
_items.feedback: The point is not about individual ability; it is that conventions differ by field.

_items.text: Because academic writing is really just the same as good writing in general.
_items.feedback: That is the assumption the lesson rejects: there is no single standard above every subject.

_items.text: Because only the sciences have strict rules for writing.
_items.feedback: Every discipline has conventions, not only the sciences; they simply differ.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic writing is not monolithic: each field sets its own conventions.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what varies between a chemist's writing and a historian's.
_incorrect.final: Academic writing is not one skill because each discipline sets its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure.

title: Formative check: analysing the difference
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's version read as disciplinary rather than generic?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's version read as disciplinary?

_items.text: It adopted the field's vocabulary and restraint and grounded the claim in a specific limitation.
_items.feedback: Yes. Same judgement, expressed in the conventions the field is marked against.

_items.text: It reached a more cautious judgement than the first student's.
_items.feedback: The judgement was identical; only its expression differed.

_items.text: It was longer and used more words.
_items.feedback: Length was not the point; the conventions of expression were.

_items.text: It avoided citing any evidence at all.
_items.feedback: It did the opposite: it tied the claim to a specific limitation.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second version read as disciplinary because it used the field's conventions and grounded the claim.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The two judgements were the same; look at HOW the second was expressed.
_incorrect.final: The second version read as disciplinary because it adopted the field's vocabulary and restraint and tied the claim to a specific limitation, not because it was longer or more cautious.

title: Formative check: identifying conventions
displayTitle: You want to identify the conventions that shape writing in {{context}}. Which approach would help most?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which approach best helps identify the conventions of a field?

_items.text: Examine how writers in {{context}} handle voice, vocabulary, structure and evidence.
_items.feedback: Yes. Those recurring choices are where a field's conventions show themselves in {{context}}.

_items.text: Apply a single checklist of good writing that works for every subject.
_items.feedback: A universal checklist misses what is specific to {{context}}; conventions are local.

_items.text: Count how many sources each piece cites.
_items.feedback: The number of sources says little about a field's conventions of style and structure.

_items.text: Choose whichever style you personally find easiest to write.
_items.feedback: Your preference is not the field's convention; you have to work out what the field expects.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a field's conventions show in how writers handle voice, vocabulary, structure and evidence.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option that examines the recurring choices writers in the field make.
_incorrect.final: To identify the conventions of {{context}}, examine how its writers handle voice, vocabulary, structure and evidence, rather than applying a universal checklist or counting sources.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Learning a discipline's conventions
body: Four steps that turn reading for content into reading as a writer.
instruction: Select each step to reveal how it works.

_items.title: Read widely in your field
_items.body: Choose published work in your discipline that is well regarded, and read it first for its argument, as you always have.

_items.title: Read it again as a writer
_items.body: Go back over the same piece attending to how it is written, not only what it claims. Slow down on the choices the writer made.

_items.title: Notice what recurs
_items.body: Look for features that repeat across several pieces: vocabulary, sentence patterns, how sources are used, and how visible the writer is.

_items.title: Write towards them
_items.body: Bring the conventions you have noticed into your own drafts, and check your writing against the published work you admire.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are each handed an unfamiliar journal article and asked to work out how writing is done in that field.

{{learner-a}} reads it once, for content, and reports back what the article found. Asked about its conventions, {{learner-a}} can only say that it was 'formal and quite hard'. The article has been read, but only as information. Its conventions stayed invisible, because {{learner-a}} never looked at how it was made.

{{learner-b}} reads it twice. The second time, {{learner-b}} ignores the findings and watches the writing: the writer rarely appears, claims are hedged and tied to data, each paragraph opens by stating its point, and sources are woven in rather than listed. {{learner-b}} can now name four conventions of the field and write towards them.

Both students read the same article. Only {{learner-b}} read it as a writer, and so could see the conventions the first student missed.

title: Aspects to examine
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: When you read a piece as a writer, these are the aspects that reveal a discipline's conventions. Work through them on a published piece in your field.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I read the piece a second time for how it is written, not what it says?
Have I noticed how visible the writer is in the text?
Have I looked at the vocabulary: technical, cautious, discursive?
Have I examined how paragraphs open and how they are built?
Have I watched how sources are brought in and used?
Have I checked whether these features recur across several pieces, not just one?

title: Formative check: reading as a writer
displayTitle: What does it mean to read published work in your discipline 'as a writer'?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does it mean to read work in your field as a writer?

_items.text: To attend to how the piece is written, not only to what it claims.
_items.feedback: Yes. Reading as a writer means watching the choices the author made.

_items.text: To read only pieces written by well-known authors.
_items.feedback: Who wrote it matters less than attending to how it is written.

_items.text: To read as fast as possible to cover more ground.
_items.feedback: Reading as a writer means slowing down on the writing, not speeding up.

_items.text: To focus on whether you agree with the argument.
_items.feedback: Agreeing or not is reading for content; conventions are about how it is made.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading as a writer means attending to how a piece is made, not only what it says.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The point is to look at HOW the piece is written.
_incorrect.final: Reading as a writer means attending to how a piece is written, its voice, vocabulary, structure and use of sources, rather than only to its content.

title: Formative check: appraising a piece
displayTitle: In the worked example, why could the second student name the field's conventions when the first could not?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why could the second student name the field's conventions?

_items.text: They read it a second time, watching the writing rather than the findings.
_items.feedback: Yes. The second reading, focused on how it was made, revealed the conventions.

_items.text: They already knew the subject better than the first student.
_items.feedback: The difference was how they read, not prior knowledge of the topic.

_items.text: They found the article easier to understand.
_items.feedback: Ease of understanding is about content, not about seeing conventions.

_items.text: They agreed with the article's conclusions.
_items.feedback: Agreement is reading for content; it does not reveal how the piece is made.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A second reading focused on the writing is what made the conventions visible.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the second student DID differently with the article.
_incorrect.final: The second student could name the conventions because they read the article again, watching how it was written rather than what it found.

title: Formative check: choosing what to notice
displayTitle: You are working out an unfamiliar convention in a text in {{context}}. Which is the most useful thing to notice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the most useful thing to notice to work out a convention?

_items.text: The choices that recur across several pieces: voice, vocabulary, structure and use of sources.
_items.feedback: Yes. Recurring choices in {{context}} are where a convention shows itself.

_items.text: A single striking sentence you happen to like.
_items.feedback: One sentence may be a one-off; a convention is what recurs.

_items.text: The length of the piece.
_items.feedback: Length rarely reveals a field's conventions of style and structure.

_items.text: Whether the topic interests you.
_items.feedback: Your interest in the topic says nothing about the field's conventions.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, a convention shows in the choices that recur across pieces.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A convention is a pattern, so look for what recurs.
_incorrect.final: To work out a convention in {{context}}, notice the choices that recur across several pieces, not a single sentence or the length of the text.

title: Read like an editor
displayTitle: Find the voices in a paragraph
body: This paragraph uses the 'voices' technique with a critical edge. Find the writer's own voice, the evidence drawn from a source, and the critical judgement.
instruction: Choose a tool, then click the marked phrase that plays that role. Mark all three, then Submit.
ariaRegion: Annotate. Choose a tool, then select phrases in the passage to mark their role.
passage: [[The case for this is not yet settled.]] Rahman (2019) reports a large effect, but [[the study covers a single site]], so [[its claim to generality is weak]].

_feedback.correct: Exactly. You have found the writer's own-voice opening, the evidence from the source, and the critical judgement.
_feedback._incorrect: Not quite. Check the notes below to see which role each phrase plays.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students use the same source, a study reporting a strong result, in a paragraph of their own.

{{learner-a}} writes: 'Rahman (2019) found a large effect. This shows the approach works.' The source is cited correctly, but it is simply reported and then accepted. The paragraph has no voice of its own: it passes on the finding and takes its conclusion as settled. This is reporting, not arguing.

{{learner-b}} writes instead: 'The case is not yet settled. Rahman (2019) reports a large effect. But the single setting limits how far it generalises.' The paragraph opens and closes in {{learner-b}}'s own voice. The source supports a point rather than making it. The language of criticality, weighing and qualifying, flags the judgement.

Both students used the same source accurately. Only {{learner-b}} made it serve an argument, and showed the reader where the criticism was happening.

title: Integrating a source with a critical edge
displayTitle: Checklist: How to do it
body: Use these questions on a paragraph of your own that draws on a source.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Does the paragraph open in my own voice with a clear statement of its point?
Is the source used to support or qualify that point, rather than to make it for me?
Does the paragraph close in my voice with what I make of the source?
Have I used the language of criticality to weigh, question or judge?
Could a reader see where I am being critical, rather than just reporting?
If I removed the citation, would there still be an argument of my own?

title: Formative check: the voices technique
displayTitle: In the 'voices' technique, what is the role of the writer's own voice in a paragraph?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the role of the writer's own voice in the voices technique?

_items.text: To open and close the paragraph, stating its point and what the writer makes of the sources.
_items.feedback: Yes. Your voice frames the paragraph; the sources serve the point it makes.

_items.text: To stay out of the paragraph so the sources can speak for themselves.
_items.feedback: That produces a report, not an argument; the voices technique keeps your voice framing it.

_items.text: To quote the sources as fully as possible.
_items.feedback: Full quotation is not the point; using sources to serve your point is.

_items.text: To summarise each source in turn, one per sentence.
_items.feedback: Listing sources in turn is what the technique is designed to avoid.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Your own voice opens and closes the paragraph and uses the sources to serve its point.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about where your own voice sits in the paragraph.
_incorrect.final: In the voices technique your own voice opens and closes the paragraph, stating its point and what you make of the sources, while the sources support that point.

title: Formative check: signalling criticality
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's paragraph read as an argument rather than a report?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's paragraph read as an argument?

_items.text: It framed the point in the student's own voice and used the language of criticality to weigh the source.
_items.feedback: Yes. Own-voice framing plus weighing and qualifying turned the source into support for an argument.

_items.text: It quoted Rahman (2019) more fully.
_items.feedback: Fuller quotation would not make it an argument; framing and judgement did.

_items.text: It left out the citation.
_items.feedback: It kept the citation; the difference was how the source was used.

_items.text: It accepted the finding without question.
_items.feedback: That is what the first student did; the second weighed it instead.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Own-voice framing and the language of criticality made it an argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at how the second student framed and weighed the source.
_incorrect.final: The second paragraph read as an argument because it was framed in the student's own voice and used the language of criticality to weigh the source, not because it quoted more or dropped the citation.

title: Formative check: advancing versus reporting
displayTitle: Appraising two paragraphs against the conventions of {{context}}, what marks the one that uses a source to advance an argument rather than merely report it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Appraising against your discipline's conventions, what marks a paragraph that advances an argument?

_items.text: The advancing paragraph frames a point in the writer's voice and weighs the source; the reporting one just passes the source on.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, an argument shows the writer's voice and judgement around the source.

_items.text: The advancing paragraph has more citations.
_items.feedback: More citations do not make an argument; how the source is used does.

_items.text: The reporting paragraph is always shorter.
_items.feedback: Length does not distinguish them; the writer's voice and judgement do.

_items.text: The advancing paragraph avoids citing any source.
_items.feedback: An argument still uses sources; it uses them to support its own point.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, the advancing paragraph frames a point in the writer's voice and weighs the source.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the writer's own voice and judgement around the source.
_incorrect.final: In {{context}}, a paragraph advances an argument when it frames a point in the writer's voice and weighs the source, rather than simply passing the source on; citation count and length do not decide it.

body: Why is it misleading to treat 'academic writing' as one universal skill?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is academic writing not one universal skill?

_items.text: Each discipline sets its own conventions for style, vocabulary and structure.
_items.feedback: Yes. Conventions are local to a field, so there is no single standard.

_items.text: Only strong students can write well in any subject.
_items.feedback: The point is about fields differing, not about individual ability.

_items.text: Good academic writing is the same everywhere once you learn the rules.
_items.feedback: That is the assumption the course rejects.

_items.text: Writing only matters in essay subjects.
_items.feedback: Every discipline has writing conventions.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Each discipline sets its own conventions, so there is no single academic writing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what varies between fields.

body: Two students express the same cautious judgement. One reads as disciplinary, the other as generic. What most likely explains the difference?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What explains one judgement reading as disciplinary and the other generic?

_items.text: One adopted the field's vocabulary, restraint and way of grounding a claim.
_items.feedback: Yes. Same judgement, expressed in the field's conventions.

_items.text: One reached a more original conclusion.
_items.feedback: The judgements were the same; only the expression differed.

_items.text: One wrote considerably more.
_items.feedback: Length is not what makes writing disciplinary.

_items.text: One used no sources.
_items.feedback: Disciplinary writing grounds claims rather than dropping sources.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Expressing a judgement in the field's conventions is what reads as disciplinary.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The judgements were identical; look at how they were expressed.

body: What does it mean to read published work in your discipline 'as a writer'?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does reading as a writer mean?

_items.text: Attending to how the piece is written, not only to what it claims.
_items.feedback: Yes. You watch the choices the author made.

_items.text: Reading only the most famous authors in the field.
_items.feedback: Fame is not the point; how it is written is.

_items.text: Reading quickly to cover more sources.
_items.feedback: Reading as a writer means slowing down on the writing.

_items.text: Deciding whether you agree with the argument.
_items.feedback: Agreement is reading for content, not for conventions.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading as a writer means attending to how a piece is made.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Focus on HOW the piece is written.

body: You want to work out an unfamiliar convention in your field. What is most useful to notice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is most useful to notice to work out a convention?

_items.text: The choices that recur across several pieces.
_items.feedback: Yes. A convention is a pattern, so it shows in what recurs.

_items.text: A single sentence you happen to admire.
_items.feedback: One sentence may be a one-off, not a convention.

_items.text: The overall length of each piece.
_items.feedback: Length rarely reveals conventions of style and structure.

_items.text: Whether the topic interests you.
_items.feedback: Your interest says nothing about the field's conventions.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Conventions show in the choices that recur across pieces.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A convention is a pattern.

body: In the 'voices' technique, how is a source meant to be used?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How is a source used in the voices technique?

_items.text: To support or qualify a point the writer makes in their own voice.
_items.feedback: Yes. Your voice frames the point; the source serves it.

_items.text: To make the point for the writer, so they need not take a position.
_items.feedback: That produces a report, not an argument.

_items.text: To be quoted at length so the reader has all the detail.
_items.feedback: Length of quotation is not the point.

_items.text: To be summarised one source per sentence.
_items.feedback: Listing sources in turn is what the technique avoids.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A source supports a point the writer makes in their own voice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Whose point should the paragraph make?

body: Which paragraph uses a source to advance an argument rather than merely report it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which paragraph advances an argument rather than reporting?

_items.text: One that frames a point in the writer's voice and weighs the source with the language of criticality.
_items.feedback: Yes. Own-voice framing and weighing turn a source into support for an argument.

_items.text: One that cites the source and states its finding as settled.
_items.feedback: Passing the finding on and accepting it is reporting.

_items.text: One that includes the most citations.
_items.feedback: Citation count does not make an argument.

_items.text: One that leaves the citation out altogether.
_items.feedback: An argument still uses the source, to support its own point.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Framing in your own voice and weighing the source advances an argument.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the writer's voice and judgement around the source.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: that writing is situated in your discipline, how to read published work as a writer to learn its conventions, and how to integrate sources with a critical edge. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one practice you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you can already do each of these on its own. The aim now is to see them as one continuing practice rather than three separate ideas, so that writing as a member of your discipline carries on through the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: bring together recognising your discipline's conventions, learning them by reading as a writer, and integrating sources with a critical edge into one practice
recognise the practice of writing within your discipline at work in a student's ongoing writing
plan how you will keep writing as a member of your discipline in your {{context}} work beyond this course

title: Concept: definition
body: Writing as a member of your discipline is those three strands working as one. First you recognise that conventions are local to your field. Then you learn them by reading published work as a writer. Then you put them to work, integrating sources with a critical edge so your writing advances an argument of your own. It is not three separate tasks but one practice you repeat each time you write.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice this is something you do every time you write, not once. Before a piece, you remind yourself what your field expects and look again at how published work in it is made. As you draft, you bring sources in to serve your argument and flag where your own judgement is at work. Each finished piece teaches you more about the conventions for the next.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a piece of writing you have coming up in your own subject. How will you work out its conventions, and where will you make sure your own argument and critical edge come through?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Writing as a member of your discipline is most useful as a continuing practice. You recognise your field's conventions, learn them by reading as a writer, and integrate sources with a critical edge, again and again across what you write. It is the practice, not any single piece, that makes your writing read as the work of an insider.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Writing as a member of your discipline works as one continuing cycle, repeated each time you write. Select each part to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Recognise
_items.body: Recognise that your field sets its own conventions, rather than following one universal standard.

_items.title: Read
_items.body: Read published work in your field as a writer, not only as a reader, to learn those conventions.

_items.title: Draft
_items.body: Draft in those conventions, using sources with a critical edge so they serve your own argument.

_items.title: Check and carry
_items.body: Check your writing against the work you admire, and carry what you learn into the next piece, so the cycle turns again.

_diagram.title: Writing as a member of your discipline

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two final-year students submit work in the same field. One writes in a general, all-purpose style, drops in a source, and reports what it says. The other recognises the field's conventions from the reading she has done, drafts in that style, and uses the source to support a point of her own. Over the year, the second student's writing reads more and more like the work of someone inside the discipline, because she treats all three strands as one practice.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: Checklist: How to keep writing as a member of your discipline
body: Use these questions on a piece you are writing, to keep the three strands working together.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Have I written for my own discipline's conventions, not a universal standard?
Have I worked those conventions out by reading published work as a writer?
Does my own voice open and close the paragraph, framing its point?
Do my sources serve my argument rather than making it for me?
Can a reader see where I am being critical, rather than only reporting?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat writing within your discipline as one practice rather than three separate skills?
body: Why is it more useful to treat writing within your discipline as one practice rather than three separate skills?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat writing within your discipline as one practice rather than three separate skills?

_items.text: Because the three strands feed each other: recognising conventions guides what you read for, and what you read shapes how you integrate sources.
_items.feedback: Yes. Each strand supports the others, so they work best as one practice.

_items.text: Because learning one of the three skills well means you can ignore the other two.
_items.feedback: Each strand needs the others; none of them stands on its own.

_items.text: Because treating writing as one practice means you never have to read other people's work.
_items.feedback: Reading published work as a writer is one of the three strands, not something the practice removes.

_items.text: Because one practice takes less effort than attending to conventions, reading and sources.
_items.feedback: It is not about less effort. The strands simply work better together than apart.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three strands feed each other, so writing within your discipline works best as one practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how recognising conventions, reading as a writer, and integrating sources depend on each other.

displayTitle: A student notices that history essays argue in the writer's own voice, reads several to confirm it, then drafts a paragraph that opens in her own voice and uses a source to support her point. What does this show?
body: A student notices that history essays argue in the writer's own voice, reads several to confirm it, then drafts a paragraph that opens in her own voice and uses a source to support her point. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student notices that history essays argue in the writer's own voice, reads several to confirm it, then drafts a paragraph that opens in her own voice and uses a source to support her point. What does this show?

_items.text: That she is running the three strands as one practice: recognising a convention, confirming it by reading, then writing to it with a critical edge.
_items.feedback: Yes. She moved through all three strands, one after another, as one connected practice.

_items.text: That she has memorised a set of rules that apply to every subject.
_items.feedback: The conventions she used belong to history, not to every subject.

_items.text: That reading published work replaces the need to write anything of her own.
_items.feedback: She still wrote her own paragraph; reading informed it rather than replacing it.

_items.text: That recognising a convention is all that matters, and the drafting is optional.
_items.feedback: Recognising the convention was only the first strand; she then read and drafted too.

_feedback.correct: That's right. She moved through all three strands as one connected practice.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at the three moves she made, one after another.

displayTitle: You want to keep writing as a member of your discipline in your {{context}} work this term. Which plan best treats the three strands as one continuing practice?
body: You want to keep writing as a member of your discipline in your {{context}} work this term. Which plan best treats the three strands as one continuing practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to keep writing as a member of your discipline in your your subject work this term. Which plan best treats the three strands as one continuing practice?

_items.text: For each piece, note your field's conventions, read published work to confirm them, then draft using sources with a critical edge.
_items.feedback: Yes. That runs all three strands together, again and again, as one practice.

_items.text: Pick one of the three strands and rely on it for everything you write.
_items.feedback: The strands work together; relying on one leaves the others undone.

_items.text: Apply one universal set of writing rules to every {{context}} assignment.
_items.feedback: Conventions are local to your field, so no universal set fits {{context}}.

_items.text: Read widely in {{context}} but keep your own drafts in a general, all-purpose style.
_items.feedback: Reading only helps if you then write towards the conventions you noticed.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Running all three strands on each piece keeps the practice going across your {{context}} work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that uses all three strands together, again and again.

title: Summative item 7 (tests co4)
displayTitle: Writing as a member of your discipline brings three strands together. Which description captures how they work as one practice?
body: Writing as a member of your discipline brings three strands together. Which description captures how they work as one practice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Writing as a member of your discipline brings three strands together. Which description captures how they work as one practice?

_items.text: You recognise your field's conventions, learn them by reading as a writer, and use sources with a critical edge to advance your own argument.
_items.feedback: Yes. The three strands run as one connected practice.

_items.text: You apply one universal standard of good writing to every subject you study.
_items.feedback: No universal standard exists; conventions are local to each field.

_items.text: You read widely but keep your drafts in a general, all-purpose style.
_items.feedback: The practice means writing towards the conventions you notice, not keeping a general style.

_items.text: You report what your sources say and leave your own judgement out.
_items.feedback: A critical edge means your own argument and judgement lead; sources serve them.

_feedback.correct: Correct.

title: Summative item 8 (tests co4)
displayTitle: A final-year student reads three articles in her field, notes how they hedge claims and foreground data, then writes a paragraph in that style that uses a source to support her own point. Which strands is she using?
body: A final-year student reads three articles in her field, notes how they hedge claims and foreground data, then writes a paragraph in that style that uses a source to support her own point. Which strands is she using?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A final-year student reads three articles in her field, notes how they hedge claims and foreground data, then writes a paragraph in that style that uses a source to support her own point. Which strands is she using?

_items.text: All three: she recognises and reads for the conventions, then integrates a source with a critical edge.
_items.feedback: Yes. She moves through all three strands as one practice.

_items.text: Only recognising conventions; she has not read or drafted anything.
_items.feedback: She did read three articles and draft a paragraph, so more than one strand is at work.

_items.text: None; writing towards a field's style is not part of writing within a discipline.
_items.feedback: Writing towards a field's conventions is exactly the practice, not a departure from it.

_items.text: Only reading; her own writing plays no part.
_items.feedback: She wrote her own paragraph using a source, so her writing is central.

_feedback.correct: Correct.
